newsitem.title: HAITI: U.S. commander reviews U.S. troop presence in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: U.S. commander reviews U.S. troop presence in Haiti.

text.p: U.S. General Wesley Clark visited Haiti on Tuesday to review the possibility of U.S. troops staying in the country after the June 1 deadline for their humanitarian mission passes.
"We believe there is some continued work to be done to improve the roads and facilities in Haiti," Clark said at a news conference before flying out.
Clark is commander in chief of the U.S. Southern Command, which covers most of Latin America and next month extends its writ to the Caribbean.
The 20,000 U.S. troops that restored former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power in 1991, three years after he was ousted by a military coup, withdrew from Haiti in March last year.

U.S. President Bill Clinton promised that all U.S. troops would leave Haiti after the 1996 presidential election. A U.N. peacekeeping mission replaced the U.S. troops, although some 500 U.S. troops remain as the U.S. Support Group charged with humanitarian work such as building roads and schools and providing medical help. Their mission expires on June 1.
U.S. soldiers have also been seen carrying out security and drug enforcement actions throughout the country.

Armed U.S. Marines were present in the slum of Cite Soleil during police actions to control gang warfare there in February. The marines said they were providinbg back-up to the U.N. and Haitian National Police.

Military sources have said the U.S. soldiers have also been involved in drug interdiction operations. A non-U.S. diplomatic source said he had witnessed U.S. Special Forces carrying out drug enforcement activities in the southern port of Jacmel.
U.S. Support Group Public Affairs Officer Lt. Stewart Upton, however, denied U.S. soldiers had been involved in any security or drug enforcement actions.
"The sole mission for the U.S. Support Group is to provide humanitarian and civic assistance," he said. "Anything outside of that would have to come under orders from a higher authority."
Any decision on extending the U.S. Support Group's mission would be made by the Pentagon, or by Clinton himself.
